sections.content: Describing a country's product means packing detail into a single sentence -- que for a thing or action, donde for a place, cuyo/cuya for a possessive link ("whose") that agrees with the noun that follows it, not with the person or thing it refers back to. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: Brasil, cuya producción de café llegó a superar la de cualquier otro país del mundo, construyó alrededor de este cultivo toda una estructura política y social.
items.english: Brazil, whose coffee production came to surpass that of any other country in the world, built a whole political and social structure around this crop.

items.spanish: El estado de São Paulo, donde se concentraba la mayor parte de las plantaciones, se volvió central en la política nacional.
items.english: The state of São Paulo, where most of the plantations were concentrated, became central to national politics.

items.spanish: Chile incorporó los territorios donde se concentraban los mayores yacimientos de salitre.
items.english: Chile incorporated the territories where the largest saltpeter deposits were concentrated.

items.spanish: El banano, un producto cuya exportación creció rápidamente en países como Costa Rica y Honduras, definiría la imagen exterior de la región.
items.english: The banana, a product whose exports grew rapidly in countries like Costa Rica and Honduras, would define the region's image abroad.

sections.content: Cuyo agrees with the noun it introduces, not the owner: cuya producción (agreeing with producción, feminine) even though it refers back to Brasil (masculine) -- this trips up learners who expect it to work like an adjective describing the owner instead.
